330.title: The ranges ahead
330.hook: four more years: the Stoics in full, the great questions, the thinkers and the practices, and your own way
330.howItsDone: People on a long path of study often pause at the end of a year to look ahead at what comes next, without committing to all of it at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday: docta ignorantia, what you still don't know. Your line: still asking.

The top of a hill has a trick it plays. You catch your breath, you look out, and you see that this wasn't the top of anything. Behind it, there's another ridge. Behind that, a range. Blue, then paler blue, all the way to the edge of the sky. For some people that moment is deflating. More climbing? For others it's the best part of the whole walk. The world is bigger than the hill. Tomorrow, year one ends. Before the last look back down, today is for looking out.
screen: `THE TOP OF THE HILL.` → `ANOTHER RIDGE, THEN A RANGE.` → `BIGGER THAN THE HILL.`

segments.voice: Year two: the porch. The Stoics in full. You met them in stories and practices; next year you read them properly, starting with Epictetus's handbook, in order, a line at a time. The school took its name from the stoa, the painted porch in Athens where Zeno taught, so year two is named for it. Year three: the great questions. Wisdom from every tradition, gathered by theme. What is a good life? How do we face death? What do we owe each other? Each tradition answers in its own words, and each is heard without ranking, the way you listened this year as a guest. Year four: the thinkers and the schools. It opens with the Tao Te Ching, chapter by chapter, the old master's short, strange book, and goes on to the philosophers and the practices that grew around them. Year five: the summit. Reading the sources yourself, walking with the poets, and finally, living your own way. By then, the path hands you less and asks more. The questions you wrote yesterday will still be there. A few may have softened. Now the honest part. Nobody knows how far you'll go. Some people walk the whole range. Some walk a year, and carry two practices for the rest of their lives, and that is a whole life's worth. The ranges aren't a to-do list. They're there, the way mountains are there: to look at, to wonder at, and to walk when you're ready. One day at a time, like this one.

segments.voice: Go to a window, or outside, and find the farthest thing you can see, a line of roofs, trees, hills, the sky's edge, and let your eyes rest there, soft and wide. Then notice your breath, right here: the far thing and the near breath, both at once. Don't plan anything; just look out.

Your line: the ranges. They can stay far for now. One day left in year one.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: year one ends: look back down the hill, then up
331.howItsDone: Many people mark the end of a long stretch of practice by going somewhere high or open, looking back over what they did, and naming what comes next.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stoa, and the ranges ahead. Your line: the ranges.

At the top of the hill there's a lookout. A flat rock, a rail, maybe a bench someone carved their initials into. This is day three hundred thirty-one of the climb. Maybe some days you ran. Maybe some you crawled. Maybe on a few you sat down on the path and didn't move, and that counted too. Below you, the whole trail, switchbacks and all, back down to the spot where you took one breath with a bell. Above and beyond, the ranges. For one day, you get to stand in the middle and see both.
screen: `A FLAT ROCK, A RAIL, A BENCH.` → `331 DAYS OF CLIMBING.` → `THE TRAIL BELOW, THE RANGES BEYOND.`

segments.voice: Look down at the camps. The first words, starting with breathe. The stories: a shipwreck, a butterfly, a carob tree. The practices: the breath, the evening review, the sunset. The text: Rumi's reed, with Marcus beside him. Then this last camp, the depths, the longest of all. You went as a guest into seven homes. Hinduism: dharma, and you are that. Buddhism: wake up, and may all beings be well. Judaism: hear, and repair. Christianity: love your neighbor, and grace. The Catholic tradition: the rosary and the works of mercy. Islam: one God, and hearts that find rest in remembrance. Sikhism: the name, honest work, and the free kitchen. Then home to the Stoic porch: character, the four virtues, the citadel. Then the lab: resonance breathing, sixty-six days, take it for a walk somewhere green, a mirror, not a forecast, and Hume's gap between is and ought. Then the doors: every door stays open. Now a line from a tradition that loved hills. A psalm, in the King James words: "I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help." The next verse answers: the help comes from God, the maker of heaven and earth. The King James Bible heads this psalm a song of degrees, and tradition links those songs with pilgrims going up to Jerusalem. And one from the Tao Te Ching, in James Legge's translation: "The journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step." You took that step on day one. Every step since was also a single step. That's all a year is. Tomorrow, the porch: year two opens with a little handbook meant to be kept at hand.

332.title: The handbook for the road
332.hook: Arrian, Epictetus' student, boiled his teacher down into a little book meant to be kept at hand
332.howItsDone: Many people who practice Stoicism keep a copy of Epictetus' Handbook nearby, or copy a single line onto a card, and reread it during the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rumi's reed, at the big lookout, the top of year one. Your line was look how far. Today, year two begins.

Most books that change lives are too heavy to carry. This one fits in a coat pocket: around fifty short sections. You can read it on a bus ride and spend the rest of your life on it. Nearly two thousand years ago, in a school on the western coast of Greece, a young man named Arrian sat writing down everything his teacher said. The teacher was an old man with a lame leg who had grown up enslaved, and he never wrote a word himself. The student wrote it all, then boiled it down. Year two opens on the porch. Today: the handbook for the road.
screen: `A BOOK THAT FITS IN A POCKET.` → `A STUDENT TAKING NOTES.` → `THE HANDBOOK FOR THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Epictetus was born around the year fifty in Hierapolis, in what is now Turkey, and grew up enslaved. His owner, Epaphroditus, was a freedman who served at the court of Nero. Somehow the young man was allowed to study with Musonius Rufus, the Stoic from year one who called plain food training. Later he was freed and taught philosophy in Rome, until the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from the city near the end of the first century. Epictetus moved to Nicopolis in Greece and opened a school. Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. Arrian, later a Roman governor and the historian of Alexander the Great, took down his teacher's talks. Those notes became the Discourses; four books survive. Then Arrian made something smaller: the best of it in short, plain sections. Enchiridion is Greek: en, in, and cheir, the hand. Something kept in the hand. The same word could mean a hand-knife, a small blade you keep close. Not a book for the shelf; a tool for the road. People have carried it ever since. Marcus Aurelius thanks one of his teachers for lending him a copy of Epictetus' notes, and Christian monks later adapted the handbook for life in their communities. This year the Stoics get read properly and in order: the handbook first, a section or two a day, then the Discourses, Seneca's letters, the whole of Marcus. They're one school among many, read here on their own terms.

333.title: What is ours
333.hook: our judgments, impulses, desires and aversions are ours; body, property, reputation and office are not (Enchiridion 1)
333.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often sort a worry into what is up to them and what isn't, sometimes on paper in two columns, and put their effort into the first.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was enchiridion, the little book kept in the hand. Your line was keep it at hand.

Page one of the handbook is not a pep talk. It's a sorting job. Two piles: into the first goes everything that is really yours; into the second, everything else. No warm-up, no story, no promise. Epictetus seems to think that if this one sorting goes wrong, nothing else in the book will help, and if it goes right, the rest will start to make sense on its own. So before it says anything about living well, the handbook asks a plainer question: what is ours?
screen: `PAGE ONE: A SORTING JOB.` → `TWO PILES.` → `WHAT IS OURS?`

segments.voice: In George Long's translation of 1877, the handbook begins: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." In our power: our opinions, our impulses toward things, our desires, our aversions; in a word, whatever is our own doing. Not in our power: the body, property, reputation, office; whatever is not our own doing. Now look what's in the second pile. Your own body. Your good name. Your job. On a list of what's mine, those might come first. Epictetus says no: your body can get sick without asking you, your reputation lives in other people's heads, your job can be taken by a letter. What you do with all of it, how you judge it, what you reach for and what you push away, stays with you. Why it matters: the things in our power, he says, are free by nature; nothing can block them. The rest are weak, slavish, easily blocked, and belong to others. Treat the second pile as if it were the first, he warns, and you'll be frustrated, and you'll blame gods and people. Then the tool. When something harsh shows up, he suggests saying to it: you are an appearance, not necessarily the thing you seem. Then ask one question: is this in my power or not? If it isn't, be ready to say: it is nothing to me. That sounds cold at first, but Epictetus means something narrower. Not that it doesn't matter, but that it isn't where your work is. Your work starts here.

Read both lists slowly, then rest your eyes on the left side and breathe.

Your line: start here. One plain question, is this in my power, and the work begins on your side of it. See you tomorrow.

334.title: Desire, gently
334.hook: for now, don't desire what isn't up to you; only choose and refuse lightly (Enchiridion 2)
334.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners add a quiet reservation to their plans, such as 'if nothing prevents me', so they can act fully while holding the outcome lightly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's translation and the two piles, what is ours and what isn't. Your line was start here.

Every want comes with a promise tucked inside it. Want the job, and the want quietly promises: you'll get it. Dread the diagnosis, and the dread promises: you'll escape it. The promise is easy to miss until it breaks, and then the disappointment can seem like something done to us. Section two of the handbook takes those promises seriously. It doesn't tell a beginner to stop wanting forever. It says something gentler, and odder, with two small words that matter a lot: for now.
screen: `EVERY WANT HIDES A PROMISE.` → `THE PROMISE BREAKS.` → `FOR NOW.`

segments.voice: Desire, Epictetus says, promises that you'll get what you desire; aversion promises that you won't fall into what you avoid. Miss what you desire and you feel unlucky. Fall into what you avoid and you feel wretched. So move aversion home. If you only push away things in your own power, like your own cruelty or cowardice, you'll never fall into them against your will. Try to avoid sickness, death or poverty, and you've signed up for misery, because those aren't yours to avoid. So he says: take aversion off everything outside your power, and set it on the things inside it. Then the surprise. For the present, he says, set desire aside completely. Desire what isn't up to you and you're bound to be disappointed, and the good things that are up to you, a steady character, sound judgment, aren't yet within a beginner's reach. This is advice for someone starting out, not a rule for a whole life. Meanwhile, use only choosing and refusing, moving toward a thing or away from it, and do even that lightly, without straining, with a reservation. The Stoics meant a quiet clause attached to a plan. Seneca gives one: I'll sail, unless something gets in the way. Neighbors say something close. Muslims say in sha Allah, if God wills, and the letter of James in the New Testament says to speak of plans with: if the Lord will. Epictetus' version is simply: lightly, and for now.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you want that isn't fully up to you, a reply, a result, a yes from someone, and feel where the want pulls in your body. 335.title: It's a jug
335.hook: if you love a jug, say "I love a jug," and if it breaks you won't be thrown (Enchiridion 3)
335.carry: clay breaks; that's part of what clay is
335.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism name a cherished object plainly to themselves, 'this is a cup, and cups break', practicing on small things first.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was desire: for a beginner, set it down for now and choose lightly. Your line was gently, for now.

A mug that nobody else is allowed to use. Chipped, maybe. A gift, maybe. Somebody's grandmother's. One morning it slips off the counter, and the small crack on the tile floor can land like bad news. Everyone in the kitchen knows it's a mug. And still. Epictetus, teaching in a Greek town, picked almost exactly this object to start with: not a great loss, a clay pot from the kitchen. Today: it's a jug.
screen: `THE MUG NOBODY ELSE USES.` → `A CRACK ON THE TILE.` → `IT'S A JUG.`

segments.voice: In section three of the handbook, Epictetus says: with everything that delights you, or is useful, or that you love, remind yourself what kind of thing it is. Start with the smallest things. If you're fond of a jug, say: I'm fond of a jug. Then when it breaks, you won't be thrown. The point isn't to love it less. You can still drink from the good mug every morning; the practice is to name it truly while you have it. Clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Said ahead of time, the breaking is a sad thing that happened, not a betrayal. Then the hard part. The same section doesn't stop at jugs. When you kiss your child or your wife, Epictetus goes on, say to yourself that you are kissing a human being, and then if one of them dies, you won't be overwhelmed. Readers argue about this line. Some find it cold, a way of guarding the heart against the people it should be open to. Others hear it as tender: everyone you love is mortal, and saying so can make each goodbye at the door count. The text itself doesn't settle it, and you don't have to either. Why start small? Epictetus is a trainer, and nobody lifts the heaviest weight on the first day. Practice on the jug, the phone screen, the favorite sweater, and learn the move where it costs little.

336.title: Going to the baths
336.hook: before going out, picture what happens at the public baths: splashing, shoving, theft, and keep your purpose (Enchiridion 4)
336.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners take a moment before an outing to picture its usual frustrations and name their aim: to do the errand and stay the person they mean to be.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus and the jug, naming what you love for what it is. Your line was clay breaks; that's part of what clay is. Today rounds off year two's first week.
screen: `CLAY BREAKS; THAT'S PART OF WHAT CLAY IS.`

segments.voice: A public bathhouse, a busy afternoon. Steam, echoing tile, a hundred voices. Somebody cannonballs into the pool and soaks your towel. Somebody shoves past you on the wet steps. Somebody shouts insults across the room. And somebody, while you're in the water, walks off with your sandals. None of it is strange for a crowded bath; it is simply what happens there. This is the scene Epictetus chooses for section four: not a battlefield, an afternoon errand. Today: going to the baths.
screen: `STEAM, TILE, A HUNDRED VOICES.` → `SPLASHED, SHOVED, ROBBED.` → `GOING TO THE BATHS.`

segments.voice: When you're about to do anything, Epictetus says, remind yourself what kind of activity it is. If you're going out to bathe, picture what happens at the baths: people who splash you, push, insult you, steal. Nothing mysterious; just honest weather for that place. Having pictured it, say to yourself: I want to bathe, and to keep my purpose in line with nature. Notice the and. You're going for a bath, and to stay the kind of person you mean to be while you're there. Then, he says, if something gets in the way of your bath, you'll have the words ready: I didn't want only to bathe, but also to keep my purpose, and I won't keep it if I'm furious about every splash. The bath can go badly and the trip can still succeed, because half of what you came for was always yours. Today's bathhouse might be the grocery store at six, the family dinner where a certain uncle will say a certain thing, the group chat, the morning commute. None of it is a surprise, and yet it can still ambush you, because you walk in expecting only the errand. A one-minute preview at the door, and an and attached to the errand, changes what counts as a good outing. And a look back at the week: year two opened with a book for the hand, then two piles, then desire held lightly, a jug, and today the baths. Each one is small enough to carry out the door.
screen: `PICTURE WHAT HAPPENS THERE.` · `I WANT TO BATHE, AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.` · `THE BATH FAILS, THE TRIP SUCCEEDS.` · `TODAY'S BATHHOUSE.` · then, large: `AND KEEP MY PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Walk through one outing ahead of you, a store, an office, a visit, a phone call, and let the usual snags appear without bracing: the line, the delay, the comment, the noise. Then say your sentence inside: I want to do this errand, and keep my purpose. Picture yourself in the middle of the worst moment, still steady.
Epictetus, previewing an errand: picture what usually happens, then go with two aims, the errand and your own purpose. Today's word.
Your line: and keep my purpose. The errand, and the purpose: two aims at every door. A week of year two, complete.
